extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, US institutional history, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the conditions, principles, and political behaviors that make the American Union and republican institutions durable or vulnerable, as argued in a 19th-century political analysis. Focuses on legal authority, popular morality, institutional structure, and social manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary as the authentic expounder of the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary is looked to as the only authentic expounder of the constitution; until a law of Congress has passed that judicial ordeal, its constitutionality is open to question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative acts are not generally regarded as authoritative expositions of the constitution except where there has been a constant and uninterrupted practice from the organization of government; historical examples illustrate when courts settled constitutional questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative weight of uninterrupted legislative practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Only very few cases where a constant and uninterrupted legislative practice exists are regarded as sound and authoritative expositions of the true sense of the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity of practice since government organization as a criterion for when congressional acts may be treated as settled constitutional interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State property rights versus federal treaty authority regarding Indians
rubrics_metrics.description: States succeeded to the crown's ownership rights in lands within their boundaries after independence; the United States' authority to make treaties with Indian tribes is conceded and does not conflict with state ownership of lands within state boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) state proprietorship of soil (subject to Indian occupancy until extinguished by purchase/cession) and (b) federal treaty-making power with tribes, especially regarding territory outside state boundaries or lands ceded to the United States; legal citations and historical practice are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: National bank as indicator of Union strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank of the United States functions as the great monetary tie of the Union; opposition to it is a symptom of declining support for the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presence and stability of national monetary institutions (e.g., a central bank) as evidence of federal cohesion; note political attacks on such institutions as evidence of provincializing tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as the core of constitutional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans form a sole and undivided people in the cases specified by the constitution; the will of the nation is expressed by the voice of the majority, and when the majority has pronounced its decision, the minority must submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about constitutional interpretation and resistance in light of the normative principle that majority decisions within constitutional bounds determine binding policy; consider how political actors justify or resist majority rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nullification undermines the federal constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that each state may judge the constitutionality of federal laws and suspend their execution (nullification) destroys the basis of the federal constitution and revives the defects of the old Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any assertion of unilateral state power to annul or refuse federal law as a criterion of institutional breakdown; historical examples (e.g., South Carolina's 1832 decree) illustrate the practice and danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: State conventions and extra-judicial annulment as a sign of constitutional crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: A state national convention that promulgates a decree annulling federal law, forbids levy of imposts, and refuses federal judicial appeals is an instance of nullification and constitutional conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the formation of special state conventions and decrees that bypass federal remedies as evidence of escalation from political dispute to constitutional crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential conduct as decisive for Union strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of the president may be a danger to the continuance of the federal government: a president who flatters the majority, tramples opponents, uses veto power frequently, or otherwise weakens representative institutions can both strengthen his personal power and weaken the presidency's capacity to sustain the Union long-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate executive behavior for tendencies to yield to majority sentiment for popularity, to arrogate responsibility, or to undermine legislative authority; balance between defending the Union and pandering to provincial passions matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican government defined by slow, deliberative, moral processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican government in the United States is the slow and quiet action of society upon itself: resolutions are allowed time to ripen, are deliberately discussed, and executed with mature judgment; the republic values morality, religion, and rights and recognizes limits on majority power (humanity, justice, reason, vested rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the health of republican institutions by the extent to which political processes are deliberative, respect moral and religious norms, and formally protect vested rights against unbounded majority action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience of the republic requires coherence of law, manners, and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To destroy republican institutions, all laws must be changed at the same time and a great alteration must take place in manners — a long series of events with the same tendency would be required to substitute opposite laws, manners, and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of alignment between legal frameworks, social manners, and prevailing opinions as a measure of a republic's resistance to radical regime change; fragmentation across these domains implies vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography and municipal traditions bolster republican permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispersed population, many natural obstacles, early adoption of municipal liberty, and settlement patterns that produced many small communities make it difficult to establish centralized administration and thus favor provincial and municipal government, strengthening republicanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural factors—territorial scale, settlement history, local governmental traditions—as protective elements for republican forms; absence of such factors increases centralizing or monarchical prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy unlikely where republican laws and manners persist
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarchy would find it hard to succeed in the United States because there is no pre-existing legislative system or set of manners prepared for it; republican laws, opinions, and habits impede the establishment of monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the feasibility of monarchical or authoritarian alternatives by checking whether supporting legal structures and social habits exist; lacking these, regime change toward monarchy is much more difficult.
